newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Donors may praise Bangladesh for reform efforts.
newsitem.headline: Donors may praise Bangladesh for reform efforts.

text.p: Donors are expected to praise Bangladesh's recent performance in impelementing economic reforms when they meet in Dhaka on Tuesday, government and aid officials said on Sunday.

The new government of Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina was trying hard to realise its commitment to donors by implementing the reform programme, the head of the World Bank mission in Dhaka, Piere Landell-Mills, told Reuters.

He said the donors, comprising 30 international agencies and countries, might at their mid-term review meeting here express praise for the government, especially for its efforts in economic development.

World Bank officials said the present government took a bold step when it appointed Syed Manzur Elahi, a leading private sector entrepreneur, as the chairman of the Privatisation Board. Elahi also served as an adviser to the caretaker government which supervised the elections last June that brought Hasina to power.

They said the government may be able to successfully transfer the loss-making state-owned Purbachal Jute Industries to a foreign company. The government spends about $500 million on subsidies and loss recovery annually.
The officials said the donors might also appreciate the government's efforts to form a bank reforms commission and to empower the financial loan court to issue and execute decrees on defaulters.
The government has already put a draft bankruptcy act before a parliamentary committee, they said.
"All these are the plus points of the present government which may draw praise from international donors," one bank official said.
The meeting will review Bangladesh's economic reforms, privatisation and aid utilisation.
Masihur Rahman, Secretary of the Economic Relations Division, said Bangladesh was not much worried about the flow of official foreign aid.
Bangladesh has opened up its economy to attract private capital from home and abroad.

Wahiduddin Mahmud, an eminent economist and the former finance and planning Adviser of the caretaker government, said: "The (two-day) mid-term review by donors is particularly signifcant in view of the existing bottlenecks in aid utilisation."
The annual aid disbursement declined to $1.45 billion in fiscal 1995/96 (July-June) from around an average $1.6 billion to $1.7 billion in recent years,
"The decline...is mainly attributed to political unrest and uncertainty," Mahmud said.
But he said the aid disbursement during July-November of the current fiscal had been estimated at about $480 million, which is an improvement on last year's situation.
"The low rate of aid utilisation may be partly due to the imposition of stricter aid conditions by donors, but also partly due to the weakness in project implementation," he said.
Mahmud said the government should either improve aid utilisation or downsize its Annual Development Plan (ADP) in furture.
